heading: Setting it up
text: Create an API key at openrouter.ai. OpenRouter is a gateway, so one key reaches models from many providers. Open Settings → AI Assistant and paste the key. There is a test button that verifies it against the provider before you rely on it. Choose a default model. The list is fetched live from OpenRouter, and you can keep a shortlist of the ones you actually use so the picker stays workable. The key is stored in your

heading: Chatting
text: Capability Detail Streaming replies Text appears as it is generated instead of after the whole answer. Model switching Change model for a conversation without changing the default. Tool use The model can call into the app to look things up and act, then continue the answer with what it found. Conversation history Chats are stored locally so you can come back to them.

heading: Where it appears
text: The assistant is a module of its own in the sidebar, and it is also available from inside a project so a conversation about that work stays next to it. Cost and privacy are between you and the provider Requests go from your machine to OpenRouter and on to whichever provider serves the model you picked. Badami does not proxy them. Usage is billed by OpenRouter on your key, and the provider's data policy applies to wha

heading: Building a request
text: The request view has a method selector and a URL field, then tabs for the rest of the request: Tab What it holds Params Query parameters. Headers Request headers. Body The request body.

heading: Collections and folders
text: Requests live in collections, and a collection can hold folders. Each collection has its own variables, so values that belong to one set of endpoints do not leak into another.

heading: Environments
text: An environment is a named set of variables. You keep one per target (local, staging, production) and switch between them with the environment selector in the request view. The variables in the active environment are what the request resolves against.

heading: Authentication
text: Badami has built-in helpers for the common schemes: Bearer token. Basic username and password. API key. You can also link a credential from the vault, so a token is never typed into a request. The credential is read at send time and the secret stays in the vault.

heading: Sending and reading the response
text: Requests run through the Rust backend, not the browser, so they are not subject to browser CORS rules. The response viewer shows the status, the headers, and the body, with a code view for the body when you want the raw form.

heading: History
text: A history panel keeps the requests you have sent, so you can go back to one and resend or edit it instead of rebuilding it.

heading: Import and export
text: Direction Format Import Postman collections. Export cURL.

heading: Scoping to a project
text: Requests can be scoped to a project. A project has its own API panel, so the endpoints for one piece of work sit with the rest of that project instead of in a single global pile.

heading: How data flows
text: The frontend never opens the database file directly. It calls Tauri commands, which the Rust side serves from the open libsql connection: A store action calls invoke("db_query", …) or invoke("db_execute", …). Kysely builds the SQL through a custom dialect whose driver is that invoke call, so queries stay type safe on the frontend. Rust runs it against badami.db, or against the sync replica when cloud sync is on. Loca

heading: Which database file is opened
text: On startup the backend picks a connection strategy so the app works offline: Situation What is opened Sync on, replica exists The replica, immediately, with no network wait. Sync on, no replica yet badami.db while the replica is built in the background. Sync off badami.db as a plain SQLite file.

heading: Local Dev internals
text: The module is split so each file has one job: File Responsibility discovery.rs Reports what binaries, datadirs, ports, and resolver entries exist. runtime_manifest.rs Reads and writes the manifest that records installed versions and their hashes. runtime_updater.rs Downloads, verifies, extracts, and installs a version from upstream. datadir_migration.rs Assesses and performs the APFS clone of a MariaDB datadir. confi

heading: Sync and machine-specific data
text: Cloud sync replicates the database, but some rows describe this machine only: binary paths, sockets, and Local Dev settings. Those tables are excluded from sync so a second machine does not inherit paths that do not exist on it.

heading: The master password
text: The vault is locked behind one master password. Everything inside is encrypted with AES-256-GCM, and the key is derived from the master password with Argon2. Unlocking the vault is what makes the entries readable; until then they are ciphertext. The vault auto-locks after a configurable idle period. The default is 15 minutes. There is also a password hint setting in case you forget the master password. One password g

heading: Credential types
text: There are nine types, each with its own secret fields: Type For Web loginSite logins with a username and password. App accountDesktop and mobile app accounts. API keyService tokens and keys. DatabaseDatabase connections. EmailMail accounts. LicenseSoftware license keys. Secure noteFree text that has to stay secret. Environment variablesKey and value pairs for a project. Server accessMachine credentials that can be li

heading: Common fields
text: Every credential also carries these fields, on top of the type-specific secrets: Name. Username. URL. Service name. Environment: Production, Staging, Development, or None. Tags.

heading: TOTP
text: A credential can hold a shared secret for two-factor codes. Badami generates the current 6-digit code and shows a countdown until it rolls over. SHA1, SHA256, and SHA512 are supported.

heading: Password generator
text: When you are creating a new secret, the generator builds a strong password for you instead of leaving you to invent one.

heading: Linking
text: Credentials do not have to stand alone: A credential can be linked to a project. A Server access credential can be linked to a server, and the server form's From Credential Manager authentication option points at it. Two separate secret stores The vault master password is separate from your operating system keychain. Server passwords live in the keychain. Vault secrets live in the encrypted vault. Unlocking one does

heading: Connections
text: The sidebar lists your saved connections. Each one holds the engine, host, port, database, username, and how to authenticate. Engine Notes MySQL and MariaDB Connects over TCP. Works with a local server or a remote host. PostgreSQL Connects over TCP, with an optional schema to open first. SQLite Opens a file on disk. No server, no credentials.

heading: SSL and SSH tunnels
text: A connection can require TLS, and can be routed through an SSH server when the database is only reachable from inside a network. The SSH side reuses the same credentials and PEM keys as the Servers module, so a host you already added there can be selected instead of retyping it.

heading: Passwords
text: Database passwords go to the operating system keychain, not into the app database. The connection row records everything except the secret. Registering the local stack If you use Local Dev, the MariaDB it manages can be registered as a connection with one click from the Local Dev panel, so the local database appears here without typing host and port by hand.

heading: Browsing objects
text: Once connected, the object browser lists schemas, tables, views, and columns. Selecting a table shows its structure and lets you page through its rows. What you can do Where Inspect columns, types, keys, and defaults The table structure view. Read rows with paging The table data view. Filter and sort without writing SQL The column headers and the filter row. Edit a cell in place Double-click a cell in the data view.

heading: Query editor
text: Each query opens in its own tab, so you can keep several statements side by side and switch between them. Results appear below the editor, and the last run stays until you run something else. Action How Run the statement The run button, or the usual keyboard shortcut for your platform. New query tab Cmd+T. Close the tab Cmd+W. See what you ran before The query history panel.

heading: Schema changes
text: Tables and columns can be created, altered, and dropped from the interface. The statement the app is about to run is shown before it executes, so a change is never applied silently.

heading: Export and import
text: Query results and whole tables can be written out, and data can be read back in. The format is chosen when you start the export.

heading: Project scoping
text: A connection can be attached to a project, which adds a Database tab inside that project so the relevant database is one click away while you work on it. Destructive statements are not sandboxed The editor sends what you write. A DROP or a DELETE without a WHERE runs immediately, against whatever connection is selected. Check the connection name before running anything that destroys data.

heading: Requirements
text: Tool Version Node.js 20 LTS or newer Rust stable, 1.77 or newer Tauri CLI v2, installed through the project's npm scripts

heading: Install Rust
text: macOS and Linux: curl --proto '=https' --tlsv1.2 -sSf https://sh.rustup.rs | sh source "$HOME/.cargo/env" rustup update stable On Windows, run rustup-init.exe and also install the Microsoft C++ Build Tools with the Desktop development with C++ workload.

heading: Platform packages
text: macOS: xcode-select --install Ubuntu or Debian: sudo apt update sudo apt install -y \ libwebkit2gtk-4.1-dev libssl-dev \ libayatana-appindicator3-dev librsvg2-dev \ patchelf pkg-config

heading: Run from source
text: git clone https://github.com/khalidinsan/badami.git cd badami npm install npm run tauri dev The first run compiles the Rust crates and takes a few minutes. Later runs are incremental. The frontend also has a browser-only dev server at npm run dev, which is useful for layout work but has no Tauri commands available.

heading: Tests
text: # Rust cd src-tauri && cargo test --lib # Frontend npm test # Types npx tsc --noEmit A few Rust tests read real machine state, such as whether a MariaDB server currently holds a datadir, and a few need a live install to copy from. Those are marked #[ignore] and run on demand: cd src-tauri && cargo test --lib -- --ignored

heading: Build release bundles
text: # Only needed to produce signed updater artifacts # export TAURI_SIGNING_PRIVATE_KEY="$(cat ~/.tauri/badami.key)" # export TAURI_SIGNING_PRIVATE_KEY_PASSWORD="" npm run tauri build Bundles land in src-tauri/target/release/bundle/: Platform Artifacts macOS .dmg, .app, plus .app.tar.gz when updater artifacts are on Windows NSIS .exe and .msi Linux .deb, .AppImage, .rpm

heading: Publishing a release
text: Version numbers live in three files and must stay in sync. A new feature phase bumps the minor version, a fix bumps the patch version. File Field package.json "version" src-tauri/tauri.conf.json "version" src-tauri/Cargo.toml version The About page reads the version through Tauri, so it never needs editing by hand. Pushing a tag runs the release workflow, which builds on macOS, Ubuntu, and Windows, publishes a GitHub

heading: Conventions
text: TypeScript runs in strict mode; the build fails on type errors. Database access goes through Kysely, not raw SQL, outside migrations. State lives in Zustand stores, one per domain. IDs are UUID v4 and timestamps are ISO strings. Icons come from Lucide React, never emoji.

heading: Where your data lives
text: Badami stores everything on your machine first. Two databases live side by side under your user account: File Purpose badami.db The local database. Always present. badami_sync.db Embedded replica, created only when cloud sync is enabled. Both sit in the app's support folder, which on macOS is ~/Library/Application Support/com.khalid.badami/.

heading: Statistics
text: The Statistics page summarises the last 30 days. There is no range selector; the window is fixed. Card What it counts Total Sessions Completed Pomodoro sessions. Total Focus Their combined minutes, shown as hours and minutes. Avg Duration Average length of a completed session. Day Streak Consecutive days ending today with at least one completed session. It reads zero until today has one, so a streak can look broken i

heading: Search and commands
text: Cmd+K opens the palette over whatever you are doing. Cmd+Shift+K opens the same search in its own small window from anywhere on the system, which is useful when Badami is not in front.

heading: What it searches
text: One query covers every module, with results grouped by type: Type Items ProjectsBy name. TasksEvery task, including subtasks. PagesProject pages by title. ServersSaved connections. CredentialsVault entries by name. APICollections and saved requests. DatabaseSaved connections. CommandsActions rather than documents.

heading: Scoping the query
text: Type a prefix to search only one kind of thing: Prefix Scope >Commands #Tasks @Servers /Projects There are also tabs across the top for the same filtering, and clicking one clears whatever you typed.

heading: Commands
text: Beyond opening things, the palette can act. Alongside navigation entries there are commands to create a project or a task, and, on macOS, to open Local Dev, start or stop the local stack, and open the Doctor. Those Local Dev commands disappear when the module is turned off.

heading: Recents
text: With an empty query, the palette lists what you used recently before anything else. That list is kept locally and holds the last ten items.

heading: Limits
text: Results are capped at 25 rows, both for recents and for a typed query. Matching is fuzzy on titles and subtitles only. It does not read the body of a page or a task's notes. The index is built when the palette opens, so something you created while it was already open appears the next time you open it. Selecting a task opens the Tasks view but does not select that task.

heading: 1. Download
text: Open the latest release and download the asset for your platform. Platform Asset Notes macOS, Apple Silicon badami_<version>_aarch64.dmg Apple Silicon only for now. Intel builds are not published. Windows badami_<version>_x64-setup.exe The .msi is available if you prefer it. Linux .AppImage, .deb, or .rpm Choose whichever fits your distribution.

heading: macOS
text: Open the DMG and drag Badami to Applications. Builds are signed so the in-app updater can verify them, but they are not notarized by Apple yet, which means Gatekeeper may refuse the first launch. Clear the quarantine flag once: # After dragging Badami to Applications xattr -cr /Applications/badami.app open /Applications/badami.app Why this is needed The signature that matters for updates is the minisign key embedded

heading: Windows
text: Run the setup executable and follow the installer. SmartScreen may warn about an unrecognized publisher for the same reason: the build is not signed with a Windows code-signing certificate.

heading: Linux
text: AppImage: make it executable and run it. chmod +x badami_<version>_amd64.AppImage ./badami_<version>_amd64.AppImage For .deb and .rpm, install with your package manager as usual.

heading: 3. Updates
text: Badami checks for a newer release on startup. You can also check by hand from About → Updates or Settings → Updates. The updater reads this endpoint: https://github.com/khalidinsan/badami/releases/latest/download/latest.json Every artifact is minisign-signed, and the public key is embedded in the app at src-tauri/tauri.conf.json. An update that does not verify against that key is refused.

heading: Uninstalling
text: Remove the app the way you normally would for your platform. If you also want to delete your data, remove the app support folder (~/Library/Application Support/com.khalid.badami/ on macOS). If you had enabled Local Dev, see Local Dev → Uninstall for the privileged pieces it can install.

PHP 8.x comes from static-php-cli and dnsmasq from a Homebrew bottle; both are verified against a published checksum before anything is unpacked. Pick the version you want. It downloads, verifies, extracts, and then runs a version check against the new binary before comm

heading: Sites
text: A parked folder serves every direct subfolder as a site, the way a web root works. A linked site points at one specific folder. Action Result Park a directory Every subfolder becomes <folder>.test. Link a project The project folder is served under its own name. Isolate PHP Pins one site to a specific PHP version through its own pool. Secure Issues a certificate from the local CA and serves the site over HTTPS.

heading: HTTP and HTTPS
text: By default nginx binds an unprivileged port, so nothing runs as root: Mode URL Requires admin HTTP, default http://mysite.test:8080 No HTTPS, per site https://mysite.test:8443 No HTTP on port 80 http://mysite.test Yes, once, to install a LaunchDaemon Port 80 is optional. Installing it writes a Badami-owned LaunchDaemon behind one admin prompt, and every config that daemon reads is rendered into a root-owned folder an

heading: Trusting the local CA
text: HTTPS works immediately, but browsers will warn until the local Certificate Authority is trusted. Settings → TLS shows the exact command it will run before the admin prompt appears, and the certificate is verified against a hash computed in the app before the keychain sees it. Removing that trust is manual: use Keychain Access, or run security remove-trusted-cert against the CA file.

heading: DNS for *.test
text: A resolver file alone is not working DNS: something has to answer on the port it points at. Badami checks by resolving a random label, not by looking for a file, and reports what it finds: Mode What happens Adopt An existing listener already answers for the TLD, so nothing is started. Badami dnsmasq Installs a dnsmasq LaunchDaemon that binds port 53. One admin prompt. High port Writes a resolver entry pointing at a n

heading: Your database
text: MariaDB reads its files from data/mariadb. If you already have a datadir elsewhere, Settings → Runtime → Database files can move it in. On APFS the move is a clone, which shares blocks with the source instead of copying them: an 11 GB datadir moves in about a second and uses almost no extra disk. The move verifies its work by hashing a sample of the copied files, always including ibdata1, and compares both sides. The

heading: Safety rules
text: Nothing is deleted automatically. Moving data clones it; removing a runtime version or a datadir is always an explicit action you take. A binary is only used if its hash matches the manifest recorded when it was installed. A half-copied or altered file reads as absent rather than as working. Starting MariaDB twice on one datadir is refused. Two servers writing the same InnoDB files is how databases get corrupted, so

heading: Uninstall
text: Local Dev → Settings → LaunchDaemon reverses what Badami installed: it removes only Badami-owned units and the staged config folder. The resolver file is removed only when you confirm and only when it carries Badami's marker, so a resolver file written by something else is left alone. To remove the whole stack afterwards, delete the folder shown at the top of this page and the root-owned folder /Library/Application S

heading: Daily Planning
text: /planning opens on a Calendar view with a Calendar / Agenda toggle above it. The calendar has previous, next, and today controls, a title, and a month / week switcher. Month is the default. Clicking a day opens the daily plan panel for that date. Dragging an event onto another day reschedules it: the drop rewrites the due date of the underlying task. Completed events render greyed out with a line through them.

heading: Agenda view
text: The agenda lists the next 30 days grouped by date. Each day header opens the daily plan panel for that date, and each task in the list carries the same three-state checkbox used elsewhere.

heading: The daily plan panel
text: The panel slides in at a fixed 320px width. Its header holds the date, an Import from project dropdown, and a close button. Below that is a summary reading N/M completed with a progress bar, then the list of rows, each with a drag handle. Click a day in the calendar, or a day header in the agenda, to open the panel. Add a plan with the Add a note... input; Enter creates it for the selected date. Schedule unscheduled

heading: What "Import from project" does
text: Choosing a project sets the due date to the selected day on every unfinished root task of that project whose due date is empty or different. It moves those tasks; it does not copy them. Subtasks and finished work are skipped.

heading: The Unscheduled pool
text: The pool lists unfinished root tasks that have no due date. Click one to schedule it on the selected day, or press Enter or Space on the highlighted row. Tasks can also be dragged from the pool into the daily list. An empty list reads No plans for this day and accepts a drop with the hint Drop to add.

heading: The Today window
text: The Today button in the sidebar opens a separate small window, 300x480 by default and 260x360 at minimum. It has no title bar, it stays above other windows, and it remembers its position and size between launches. The header shows Today with a completed over total counter and a progress strip. While a task is focused, a Focusing badge appears next to it.

heading: Window controls
text: Control What it does Font size Steps through three sizes. The whole window scales with it, because the sizes are relative. Change color Six palettes: Default, Yellow, Green, Pink, Purple, Slate. Filter by project All Tasks, Inbox, and each project that has tasks, with counts. Pin Pins or unpins the window on top. Refresh Reloads the list. Close Closes the window.

heading: The list
text: The list splits into an Overdue section and a Today section. Hovering a row reveals its actions: set priority (Urgent, High, Medium, Low, or None), assign a project, Focus, and Delete. Clicking a row title expands it. The expanded row contains a notes editor, subtasks (Enter adds one, Escape cancels), a due date picker, a due time input, and an Open in Tasks button. Add note reveals a quick-add input that supports an

heading: Pomodoro
text: A Pomodoro toggle sits in the footer. While the timer runs, a compact mm:ss chip shows in the window. The timer itself offers Reset, Play/Pause, and Skip, a progress ring, a label that reads Ready, Focus, Break, or Paused, an N sessions today count, and a back button. Focusing a task starts the pomodoro automatically when it is idle. When the session ends, a bar appears with Mark Done and Keep Going.

heading: Keyboard
text: These work only while the Today window has focus, and they are ignored while you are typing in a field. Key Action nOpen quick add. EscapeCollapse the expanded row, then clear the selection. ↑ / ↓Move the selection. SpaceToggle the selected task's status. eExpand or collapse the selected row. fFocus the selected task, and start the pomodoro. pExpand the selected row. Delete / BackspaceDelete the selected task.

The pin button changes the live window, but the choice is not remembered. Open in Tasks shows and focuses the main window, but it does not select the task there. A "note" is a task There is no separate notes table. A plan you add in the daily panel is stored

heading: How authentication is resolved
text: When a session connects, the credential is resolved in one of these ways: A password read from the keychain. A PEM file path used directly. A saved PEM key decrypted from storage. A PEM file plus a passphrase read from the keychain. A linked credential whose password field is decrypted from the vault.

text: Sessions open in a full-page view with one tab per session, and each tab shows a status dot. The + menu lists every server with SSH, Files, and IDE buttons. Closing the last tab returns you to the list.

heading: Pomodoro Timer
text: These set the length of each phase. The value in force when you start a session is saved with that session, so changing the length later does not rewrite history. Setting Default Range Work duration 25 minutes 1 to 120 Break duration 5 minutes 1 to 60

heading: Today Window
text: Setting Default Effect Always on top by default On Intended to control whether the floating Today window stays above other windows. See the note below. This toggle does not currently do anything The Today window is created always on top regardless of this setting, and its own pin button changes only the live window without saving the change. Treat the window as always on top for now.

heading: System
text: Setting Default Effect Launch at login Off Registers Badami as a login item so it is running when you log in. Close to system tray On Closing the window keeps Badami running in the background, so reminders and sync keep working. Turn it off to quit on close. Show app in Dock On Whether Badami appears in the macOS Dock.

heading: Updates
text: Shows the current version and checks GitHub Releases for a signed build. When one is available, download and install, then the app restarts. The update is verified against a signing key embedded in the app, so a build that does not match is refused.

heading: Credential Vault
text: Setting Default Effect Auto-lock timeout 15 minutes Locks the vault after this much inactivity, so a walk away does not leave it open. Password hint Empty A reminder shown on the unlock screen. Stored in plain text, so do not put the password itself there.

heading: PEM Keys
text: Manage the private keys used for SSH authentication: import a key, give it a name, and optionally store a passphrase. Imported keys are encrypted at rest. A saved key can then be chosen as the authentication method on a server.

heading: Local Dev
text: Settings, Doctor, and the runtime controls for the local PHP stack live in the Local Dev tab. They are covered in full on the Local Dev page: Setting Default Effect HTTP port 8080 The port nginx binds. Saving a new value regenerates config and restarts nginx. Default PHP version 8.4 Used by sites that are not pinned to a version of their own. TLD test The domain suffix for every local site. Loopback address 127.0.0.1

heading: Where settings are stored
text: Everything on this page is a row in the settings table inside your local database, except the values that belong to the operating system: login item registration, and server passwords and PEM passphrases, which live in the keychain. Settings that describe this machine, such as the Local Dev paths and ports, are excluded from cloud sync so a second computer does not inherit paths that do not exist on it.

text: Key Action /Open the block menu in a rich text editor. EnterSubmit a dialog or an inline field. EscapeCancel a dialog, a rename, or an inline add. One system-wide shortcut Cmd+Shift+K is the only shortcut Badami registers with the operating system, so it is the only one that can conflict with another app. Everything else works while Badami is focused.

heading: How it works
text: Badami keeps a local database on each machine and an embedded replica of your remote Turso database beside it. Writes go to the local file first and replicate in the background, which is why the app stays fast and keeps working with no network. Situation What opens Sync on, replica already exists The replica, immediately. No network wait on startup. Sync on, no replica yet The local database while the replica is buil

heading: Turning it on
text: Create a database at turso.tech. Open Settings → Cross-Device Sync, turn sync on, and paste the database URL. On the second computer, use the same URL. Its replica is created from the remote copy on first run.

heading: What syncs, and what does not
text: Documents and records replicate: projects, pages, tasks, labels, credentials, servers, API collections, and database connections. Some things deliberately stay on the machine that made them: Not synced Why Secrets in the operating system keychain Server passwords and PEM passphrases are held by the system keychain and are never part of the database, so they cannot replicate. heading: Working with a task
text: Action How Add a task Type in the input at the top and press Enter, or press n to jump to it. Change status Click the checkbox. It cycles To Do, In Progress, Done, and back. A cancelled task also returns to To Do when clicked. Add a subtask Hover a row and click +, or use the row menu. Enter adds, Escape cancels. Open the detail panel Click the task. Escape closes it. Reorder Drag a row, but only while the sort is se

heading: The detail panel
text: Clicking a task opens a panel on the right with everything about it: an editable title, a notes editor, and a properties section you can show or hide. Property Values Status To Do, In Progress, Done, Cancelled Priority None, Low, Medium, High, Urgent Project No project, or any project Due date and time A date, plus an optional time Estimate Free text that accepts 45m, 2h, or 1h 30m. A bare number is read as minutes.

heading: Subtasks
text: Subtasks nest inside their parent and can be collapsed. Nesting stops at three levels: once a task is two levels deep, the option to add another child is no longer offered. Completing a task marks every task underneath it as done at the same time. Reopening a parent brings back only the parent; the children stay done.

heading: Repeating tasks
text: Give a task a recurrence rule and a due date, and completing it creates the next occurrence on the following date the rule produces. The new task carries over the title, notes, priority, project, due time, estimate, and nesting, and it is linked back to the task it came from. The presets cover daily, weekly, weekdays, and monthly. The rule is stored as a standard calendar string, so it survives a round trip through s

heading: Reminders
text: Add one or more date and time pairs to a task. Badami checks for due reminders once a minute and raises an operating system notification, so it works whether or not the window is in front. A reminder is marked as sent once it fires, and the panel shows that next to it. Reminders are separate from due dates. A task can be due on Friday and remind you on Thursday evening.

heading: Filtering, sorting, grouping
text: Control Options Search Matches task titles. It does not search notes. Filters Status, priority, project, and label chips, plus a due date range. Clear all resets them. Sort Manual, Due Date, Priority, Title, Date Created Group by No grouping, or by project. Groups act as drop targets for dragging. Hide done Toggles finished tasks in and out of the list. heading: Board view
text: The board has four fixed columns: To Do, In Progress, Done, and Cancelled. Drag a card into another column to change its status. A quick click selects the task instead of dragging it.

heading: Labels
text: Manage labels opens a dialog where you can add a label with a name and color, and delete the ones you no longer use. Deleting a label removes it from every task that carried it; the tasks themselves stay.

heading: Install
text: Prebuilt installers for macOS, Windows, and Linux are attached to every release. The in-app updater keeps them current from there. Platform File to download macOS, Apple Silicon badami_<version>_aarch64.dmg Windows badami_<version>_x64-setup.exe or .msi Linux .AppImage, .deb, or .rpm Full walkthrough, including the first-launch step on macOS, is in Install.

page: Everything you work on,in one window.
heading: Build it yourself
text: Badami is a Tauri v2 app: a Rust backend with a React and TypeScript frontend, storing everything in SQLite on your machine. git clone https://github.com/khalidinsan/badami.git cd badami npm install npm run tauri dev The first build compiles the Rust crates and takes a few minutes. Setup per platform, the project layout, and how releases are cut are in Development.
